text: 8. Jaun. kuluṇɔ ‘to singe’, Garh. kulalyāṇ ‘smell of burnt cloth’ (Bhatt 1975 [vikrama 2032]: 78, containing as second component derivation < OIA ghrāṇá- ‘smell’), Bng. kullɔ n.m. ‘live coals, embers’ and kulliṇɔ ‘to glow; braise’, and probably kaīl adj.,n.f. ‘dirty, sooty; dirt (on body), soot’ — Pal. keriˈšpīka ‘spark’, Kal. kuluspík ‘sparks, flying ember’, Dm. kiliˈṣpik ‘spark’ (regarding the second component in Phal., Kal. and Dm. there is probably a parallel in Kṭg. phéu and Jaun. féú ‘burning particle of wood or charcoal’, and cf. Sak. ṣpargga ‘flashing’ and Psht. spaṇkay ‘spark’ perhaps < PIE *spereg- ‘to twitch’). The Bng. noun is also found as first component in kullāṇ ‘a bad smell, stench’ which is thus also composed of kullɔ plus < OIA ghrāṇá- ‘smelling’ (4531). The first component can neither be derived < kokila-² ‘lighted coal, charcoal’ (3484) nor < OIA kūḍayati, kūḷayati ‘burns’ (3399) because of the -ll-, but cf. Bng. kuḍḍɛṇɔ ‘to glow’ and kuḍāṇ ‘burnt smell (of rice)’ which are not < OIA kūḍayati but < Dhātup. and Pa. kuṇḍati ‘burns’. Very frequently, geminates in Bng. indicate the assimilation of two formerly different consonants (e.g. Bng. kallɔ ‘nettle’ is pronounced in neighbouring Deog. as karla ‘nettle’ and in Garh. as kāḷḷī [see 2804]). For kullɔ I therefore postulate Proto-Bangāṇī *kurlɔ where the -lɔ is a grammeme. kur- is indeed found in the following Bng. word: kurdāṇɔ ‘to fire the smith’s hearth with a a thick bark called bɔkɔ̄ṭh’. The bark comes from the sɔrēl pine tree. It is probably the same as Garh. kuryoṇu ‘to collect and burn all brambles & worthless objects of the field’. Instead of Bng. kurdāṇɔ also khurdāṇɔ with same meaning is common, and there are Chin. khorā ‘fireplace’ and kharā ‘oven’, Bro. khəro ‘blacksmith’ as well as S. khūro, khūrī and Jaṭ. khūrā both ‘furnace’, and Ko. khòrn ‘furnace; oven’. Here most likely also Kal. kụ ‘singed’. Note also Pers. kūr ‘a smith’s forge’, Yid.-Mj. kūra ‘the mouth- piece of a blacksmith’s bellows(?)’ and Brah. kūra ‘small furnace for smelting’. There exists a similar word with similar meaning, but only with initial aspiration: Bng. and Deog. khɔrād ‘fire not used for cooking but for other works (e.g., in a smithy)’ which, as an additional possibility, can be further compared with Oss. Iron dialect kʷyrd and Digor dialect kurd both ‘smith’ which Blažek (2008: 76) explains: “. . . may reflect the nomen agentis *kur-ta(r)- from the root attested in Gothic haúri ‘coal’, Old Norse hyrr ‘fire’ (*kurȋo-), Slavic *kuriti ‘to smoke’ (*kourȋe/o-).” To express in Bng. the activity ‘to fan such a khɔrād fire’ one uses the verb laṇɔ ‘to attach’. Whereas Bng. khɔrād is quite close to the forms quoted by Blažek and thus with PIE *kūrd-, the word kullɔ may reflect the common change of a > u which allows to postulate a form *kāra-la (with *kāra- as a side-form of OIA *skāra- ‘live coal’). Neither this nor the slightly shortened form *kārla has a permitted syllable structure in modern Bng. In other words, the original long vowel had necessarily to be shortened. *skāra- ‘live coal’ is, in a way, a common Indo-Iranian word, but the correct PIIr. reconstruction is given below in note (c). However, when we look at the geographical distribution of its derivations – together with *kāra- without initial s- – we only find Sh. and Tor., and now Bng., Chin., Bro., S., and Jaṭ. (but note also P. kerī ‘very small pieces of charcoal’ [T. Graham Bailey 1938: 246], Gau. kēr ‘soot’ and Garh. kīru ‘dhuẽ kī kālikh – soot from smoke’). Yet, within Iranian the lemma is quite widespread. Elfenbein, MacKenzie and Sims-Williams mention (2003: 74) Pashto, Persian, Sogdian and Os- setic, and I add tentatively Wakhi šokārč ‘coal, ashes’. So are the IA forms borrowings from Iranian? But why then were they apparently not borrowed into any Nuristan language? Moreover, it is strange that all Iranian reflexes only derive from the s- prefixed form, whereas the IA examples derive both from the prefixed and the non- prefixed form. However, the k- - kh- alternations quoted by Turner sub 3055 and 13649 look suspiciously similar to the situation in Bng., and all aspirations might be ‘sponta- neous’. Thus there is the question: are here the reflexes of two different PIE lemmata? Notes: (a) Perhaps also the following Bng. words are here cognate: kurāḷi ‘a clearing in the forest’ and kurāḷiṇɔ ‘to slash and burn’. In former times, such clearings were made through slash and burn (now forbidden). Thus the kur- of this word can be the same as the above one, and the second part might be a causative suffix or another extension. There is a line in an à̄rul song in which the hero says that, when his enemy did not appear for the appointed fight, he – the hero indicates ironically – found peace by burning a clearing in the forest: khodi-kurāḷiɛ kɔrilɛ sidɔ bàia dig-slash/burn.CON make.FUT.3.PL peace brother.VOC ‘Having dug and burned (the wooded area) peace (quietude) will be (with me), oh brother’ (b) Sh.pales. khá̄ro ‘live coal’ and Tor. khōr ‘ashes’ (if a genuine reflex) display common development of OIA sk > MIA kh (Pischel § 306). There is, however, Dm. čur ‘embers’ which displays a historical stage similar to the change of PIE *skend- ‘to shine’ > OIA ścandrá-/candrá- ‘shining, radiant’. It is thus more archaic than the Sh.pales. and Tor. forms. (c) Under entry ‘charcoal’, M. Heydari-Malayeri writes (2007): “[Persian] Zoqâl ‘live coal, charcoal,’ variant sokâr; Sogd.[ian] askâr; Pashto skor-; Khotan Saka skara, probably ultimately from Proto-Ir. *uz-gar-, from *uz- ‘out’ . . . + *gar ‘to heat, kindle fire, cook;’ cf. Tabari [Mazanderani] kalə ‘furnace,’ kəlen ‘ash;’ [Kurdish dialect] Laki koira; Kurd. kulan, kulandan ‘to cook;’ related to garm ‘warm;’ cf. Skt. ghar- ‘to burn,’ PIE root *gwher- ‘to warm, be warm’ . . . ” This etymological proposal – if it holds – suggests that Turner’s reconstruction *skāra- applies only to a later and geographically more restricted level. (d) It seems that the lemma has been borrowed into Munda. If so, it would be another example for early IA borrowings into Munda (more examples are found p. 896): So. kudɑː-n and contracted ˈkul-ən ‘an oven’ as in ər-əbuː-lɑːŋ-kul-ən ‘a blacksmith’s furnace’ (built with luɑːŋ-ən ‘iron’). Ramamurti observes fur- ther (1938: 147): “kulɑː-n, instead of kudɑː-n is used in children’s language; cf. Mundari -id-kula-, ‘a rough fire place formed of three stones or clods of earth”’ (see these forms also quoted sub Pinnow 52 who rightly doubts further AA con- nections; for Mu. Pinnow gives iˈdkula, iˈdkulaʔ, iˈdkulaʔd ‘rough fireplace’).

text: 15. Bng. ċɔ̀̄ n.f. ‘puddle, pool, plash’ and perhaps with an -r suffix ċɔ̀̄r n.f. ‘a small pond’, Deog. ċɔ̄ ‘waterplace for cattle’ and cɔ̄r ‘a hollow wooden log with a lid to keep water cool in summer (a traditional device)’, and Jaun. cɔ̄l ‘pond’ — Paš. čā ‘well, pool’, Dara. čʌkʌṛ ‘pond’, Wg. ċor ‘pond, pool’ (Z.), Ash. čā ‘a well’ ← Pers. cāh ‘water well’ probably partly via similar forms in many Eastern Iranian languages (like e.g. Shgh. čā ‘a well’). But some of the forms, e.g. Bng. ċɔ̀̄, may derive or are influenced by OIA cyota- ‘oozing, sprinkling’ (4947) and note here Bng. ċɔ̄ṇɔ v.i. ‘to seep or ooze away, soak’ which is < OIA cyótati ‘trickles, oozes’ (4948). Notes: (a) Cf. also Brah. čurri ‘streamlet’, Brah., Bal., Psht. čur ‘small hill-stream’ (Brah. also jhur borrowed ← OIA *jhāra- [5373] ‘flowing’) which compare with OIA curī- ‘small well or reservoir near a well’ (4873); regarding Brah. čurro ‘urine’ see (p. 591). (b) Cf. also with similar meanings Bal. čāt, čʰāθ ‘well, spring’ (Korn [2005: 227]) and Wkh. cal ‘humid, viscous’, and Kho. cat ‘pool, lake’ the last of which Mor- genstierne regards as a borrowing from a Proto-Wakhi form (1926: 76). However, later-on (1936: 660) he quotes Kho. čat, čhat and Kal. c̣hʌt both ‘lake’ (but Trail and Cooper have čhat) and says that borrowing from an Iranian language is “very doubtful.” (c) In case of Brah. čurro ‘urine’, very similar Bur. (child language) ćúro ‘urine’ and, also with meaning ‘urine’, Bng. ċɔra n.m. ‘water; cow’s urine’ and Garh. careṇḍu ‘a pond caused by cattle’s urine’ (with second component -eṇḍu < *ḍhaṇḍha- ‘mud, pool’ [5578]) and cirāṇ, carāṇ ‘stink of urine’ (with -āṇ < OIA ghrāṇá- ‘smell’) there might be contamination of reflexes of OIA *kṣarā- ‘water’ (3662) and an Austro-Asiatic lemma: cf. Monic Nyah Kur crúh ‘urinate’ and per- haps Semelai chɒ̃r ‘be urinated on’ (also ʄrʄɒr ‘urinate’) and Pacoh sṵr ‘sound of poured water, e.g. urinating into water’. Sant. caraʔc curuʔc ‘the sound of milk falling into the pail in small quantity’ and similar forms expressing sounds of dripping are probably closer to ideophones discussed pp. 591 and 257. (d) Old Him. carā, calā, caḷā ‘watercourse, channel’ (Chhabra [1957: 183]) might here not be cognate but just a reflex of OIA CAR ‘move’.

text: 43. Quite rarely also words borrowed from Arabic are found where it is not always clear how they found their way to Northwest South Asia. Two examples: (a) Bng. dureṭu n.m. ‘earring for men’, Deog. durēṭu ‘ditto’, Him. droṭu ‘earrings’ — K. dūr² ‘an earring or ear pendant, esp. one with a single pearl set in it and worn on the lobe of the ear’ — Brah. durr, Jaṭ. and Bal. dur, Si. durᵘ all ‘ear-ring’, found also in H. and ← Ar. durr ‘earring set with a single pearl’. (b) Bng. mātɔ̄2 n.m. ‘assistant of a ṭhaṇi Rajput (who is assistant of a Brahman priest in a temple of God Mahasu)’ (with -t(ɔ)1 suffix?), Deog. māta ‘assistant in a temple; servant or farmhand’. The basic meaning of mātɔ̄2 is undoubtedly ‘servant, farmhand’ because of Bng. māti n.f. ‘maidservant’ and because of the probably related Kann. māthī ‘sweeper, house-cleaner’. For instance, in the PAN epic Gandhari has a māti ‘maidservant’. The word is also found in H. mātahat ‘a subservient’, Garh. māti ‘slavery’ and Klm. mātehti LH ‘subordination’ and is a borrowing ← Ar. mā taḥt.

text: 40. Pal. keriˈšpīka ‘spark’; Kal. kuluspík (also kulušpík, kulišpík) ‘sparks, flying ember’; Dm. kiliˈṣpik; Pr. anig išpīg ‘spark’ are probably compounds with first element re- lated with the ‘(char)coal’ words discussed p. 768 sub Jaun. kuluṇɔ ‘to singe’ (except Pr. which reflects agní- ‘fire’); second element is probably cognate with Sak. ṣpargga- ‘noise, twang’ which reflects PIE *spr̥ə̑-g- ‘crackle, sputter’. These old compounds thus appear to have an original meaning like ‘live coal spatter’. They must not necessarily be Iranian borrowings. Notes: (a) Similar looking OIA sphuliṅga- ‘spark’ is not a cognate of the above forms. In KEWA Mayrhofer quotes Burrow who suggests relation with PIE *spr̥ə̑-g-; he rightly does not repeat this suggestion in EWA. This sphuliṅga- is part of a complex and not very transparent word field with elements of Indo-Aryan and Austro-Asiatic roots. In Zoller (2018: 337ff.) I have attempted to disentangle this complex. (b) Partly similar Brah. prišk ‘spark’ and Orm. spōx ‘live coal’ are difficult to connect here.

text: 64. N. chicimiro ‘the male of the white ant’ and dhamiro ‘white ant, termite’; regarding chici- cf. Kinn. chichá (cchi-cchá) ‘white mud (used for whitewashing)’, Bng. ċhiċɔ ‘lime’ (see p. 324) and Par. čhačǟ ‘white’ probably (at least the Bng. word) < OIA śvitra- (12772) and affrication of the initial sibilant which semantically parallels Jaṭ. sivvī ‘white ant’ which is < OIA śvetá- ‘white’ (12774) like Pa. suve- < OIA śvás ’tomorrow’ [Geiger § 54]); regarding N. dha- cf. OIA dhavalá- ‘dazzling white’ (6767) and Rj.jaip. dīval (note loss of aspiration!) and Garh. dhivāḍu both ‘the white ant’ (with typical change a > i), and regarding N. -miro cf. Garh. mūrā ‘a small poisonous worm appearing in the rainy season’, Kul. mukōḍi ‘ant’ (pahari-languages.ru) with - kōḍi perhaps fusion of OIA kŕ̥mi- ‘worm, insect’ (3438) and kīṭá- ‘insect, worm’ (3193), Ko. mūi and M.coch. mũ̄yĩ both ‘ant’ and kāṇṭmui ‘black ant’, and PIE *morwi- etc. ‘ant’. But because of Brah. mōrīnk ‘ant’ also old borrowing from Pers. is possible (more Iranian reflexes are quoted by Cheung [2011: 195]); moreover, even Munda origin may be possible, cf. e.g. Mu. mui ‘ant’ and see Pinnow 130. OIA lex. markoṭa-pipīlikā- ‘small black ant’ (see p. 857) is hardly related.

text: 102. The following ‘breast’ and ‘nipple’ nursery words are difficult to classify historically (a) Voiceless: Dari. pipri ‘breast; nipple’, Kho. pap ‘breast, udder’ < PIE *pap- ‘breast’ which “. . . looks like a continually reinvented children’s word. . . ” (Mallory and Adams 2006: 181); cognate is also OIA lex. pippala- ‘a nipple’. Reflexes in Germanic are Swedish and dialectal Norwegian pappe ‘woman’s breast’ and Norwegian pupp ‘tit’, Eng. pap ‘nipple’, also Lith. pãpas ‘nipple; tit; sugar-tit’. Note: Kann. pipi ‘breast’, Paṭṭ. papa ‘breast’, Lad. pipi ‘breast’, Pur. pipī(h) ‘woman’s breast, nipple’, Tib. pi-pi ‘nipple; teat’ and New. pi-pi ‘nipple’ look closer to the Indo-Aryan forms than to reflexes of #3459 PTB *pa ‘breast, nip- ple, milks’ (see STEDT). (b) Voiced: OIA *bubba- ‘woman’s breast’ (nursery word) (9283) with modern reflexes in L., N., Kṭg.; S. bubo ‘breast; dug, teat’ obviously derives < *bhubha- as found in it’s Kacchī dialect bhubho ‘woman’s breast’. Here to be added are K. bab ‘the nipple, pap, or breast of human beings, esp. of women. . . ; the udder or dugs of an animal’, Mult. bubā ‘breast’, Brj. bobā ‘nipple, breast’, P. bubā ‘a woman’s breasts’ and Marw. boba ‘female breast’ — Iranian Wkh. bap, bāp ‘woman’s breast’ — Austro-Asiatic Proto- Khmuic *buʔ ‘nipple’ or Proto-Mon-Khmer *ʔbuuʔ ‘to suck at the breast’. (c) Sub PIE *pu-p- extension (or partial reduplication?) of PIE *p(ʰ)eu- ‘blow’ Poko- rny lists Vulgar Latin *puppa, French poupe, Italian poppa all ‘nipple’, Old Ish. ucht ‘breast’ and Latv. pups ‘woman’s breast’. Notes: (a) Semantically parallel OIA *cuccu- ‘nipple’ (4855) has modern reflexes only in Nuristani, Dardic, in Balti čuču ‘mother’s breast’ and many other TB languages (in fact, STEDT reconstructs #5539 PTB *dzy(ə/o)w ‘suck; kiss; breast; milk’), West Pahāṛī Chin. and Bhad. ċiċu ‘nipple of the breast’, whereas its side-form *cucci is found in all Pahāṛī groups and in the Inner Languages, but not in the Outer Language with the exception of Gujarati. Another side-form is found in a number of Iranian languages like Ishk. cici, Sang. ciji ‘bosom’ and Oss. dzidzi, dzedze ‘nipple, breast’, in Brah. jījī ‘mother’s breast’ which resemble P. jījī ‘a woman’s breasts used by a mother in suckling’; cf. also P. cīcā ‘a woman’s breast; vulva’ and more similar forms even in Greek and Georgian quoted in Novák (2013: 188) and, more distantly related, Klm. ḍaḍ Ly ‘breast, chest’ and Sh. ḍŭḍŭˈrŭ ‘nipple, teat (woman, animal)’ (ODER reflektiert das older *juj(u)?), tĭtīˈrŭ ‘one of the two breasts’(?) titíro ‘breast’. This makes it likely that the word is a substrate or Nostratic word and therefore perhaps also Gothic *daddjan ‘suckle’ and Swab. dutte ‘female breast and nipple’ (von Schmid) (Old High German tutta). Bomhard reconstructs PN *ʒuʒ-a ‘nipple, breast’ (CINCL 298). Further parallels are Tib. čučuˑ ‘nipple’, Old Kuki ču ču mur ‘nipple’ etc.; note also Com- mon Kartvelian *ʒuʒ-u ‘woman’s breast’, Old Georgian ʒuʒu-j, ʒuʒu-js-mṭe  ‘foster-sibling (fed by same breast)’, Zan (Megrelian) ʒuʒu ‘woman’s breast’, ʒiʒ-a//ʒiʒ-e ‘wet-nurse’; note also Common Kartvelian *cic- ‘breast’, Zan cic-i ‘breast’, Common Sindy *cʷəcʷă ‘woman’s breast’, Bats ʒiʒi ‘woman’s breast’ (compared by Chukhua [2021: 97] with ancient Hurrian *zizi ‘breast, nipples’), Kabardian c əc ă ‘woman’s breast’, c əc ə-w ‘infant’ (regarding latter seman- tics cf. Ind. čičú̄ ‘a small boy’s penis’ which ). Finally, note also dialectal Germ. zuzeln ([ʦuʦəln]) ‘to suck out’. (b) It is unclear whether here related is also Ind. čičú̄ ‘a small boy’s penis’, Arm. čuč ‘penis’ and Zan (Megrelian) ḳuč̣-u ‘child’s penis’.

text: 104. Kgr. pukkā (also Maṇḍ.), pokā ‘kiss’, Gadd. and Cur. phōkū ‘kiss(es)’, Central Pahāṛī (Ku.) bhukki, bhuki ‘kiss’ (Sharma [1983: 75]), Garh. bhukkī ‘kiss; cheek’, Sirm. pŏkṭī ‘kiss’, Haṇḍūrī dialect of Kiũṭh. pūkā ‘kiss’, Pang. and Pāḍ. phă̄cī ‘kisses’ — Ind. pòk- pokʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to produce a kissing sound’, Bur. poq ét- ‘to make a kissing sound’, Sh. pok-pók ‘ditto’ — Marw. bakō and Rj.mal. bōkō ‘kiss’, Bhil. poet. buskā devā ‘to kiss’ — Nih. bukki ‘kiss’ — Brah. buk ‘kiss’. Here probably also Sh.gil. “ma bòtze” ‘kiss’ (Leitner), bōtsȋ ‘ditto’, Bro. bōšē ‘kisses’, Tor. and Klm. bēs ‘kiss’, Dir. “pùch de” ‘give a kiss”, Paš. pačū ‘kiss’ (see also note [a] below), Kho. bočhík ‘to kiss’ — Orm. pọ̄č ‘kiss’ — Gaw. poṭe-θlites ‘kissed’ (LSI [viii, ii: 87]) resembles Chatt. poṭār-ke ‘having embraced’ (LSI [i,i: 238]), K. pūtu ‘kiss’ and similar Kt. patati ‘having kissed’ (Morgenstierne [1929a: 275], not found with Strand), Ind. ˈbūīčh ‘kiss’, Pal. búusi ‘kiss’, Sh. bóċo in bóċeṭ va-, bóċyeṭ va- ‘to meet ‘to come for a single kiss” and bóoċi ‘kiss’, K. bōsa, Pr. ā-picō-kso ‘he kissed’ (LSI [viii, ii: 64, 66]) and apič, apüč- ‘to kiss’, Kt. spč- or sapčé- or supči- ‘to kiss’, Kal. išpaḍék ‘to kiss’ and saváž hik ‘to kiss’ the latter of which has a parallel in Bashg. supča ‘kiss’ — probably Bro. čipādis ‘to kiss’ (with -dis ‘to give’) and Psht. čapaī ‘kiss’ (cf. with metathesis H. paccī ‘kiss’) — G. buccī and basī ‘kiss’, Him. bhũcu ‘sucked or licked’, Garh. pucārnu ‘to kiss, caress, fondle’, Rj.ajm. bācyō ‘kiss’, Bhil. bōkī ‘kiss’ (LSI [ix: 37]), bācyā ‘kisses’ (LSI [ix: 33]), bōsī ‘kisses’ (LSI [ix: 16]), P. and H. bosā ‘kiss’ and Ko.kaṇ. bos ‘kiss’ (all three ‘borrowings’ from Pers. bos ‘a kiss’, buss (in comp.) ‘kissing’).  Notes: (a) Indirectly connected are also Paš. muču and māṣˈū both ‘kiss’ (which also has čapū ‘kiss’), Sh.gur. māči ‘kiss’, Khaś. muċākā ‘smacking of lips or a hearty kiss sound’, H. macchī ‘kiss, buss’, Psht. mača and Par. mačī both ‘kiss’ which are borrowings ← Pers. māč. K. myūṭhu ‘kiss’, N. mukh miṭhyāuni ‘to smack the lips’ and note Pur. mikhi ‘kiss’ and Munda Kor. mukka ‘kiss’ — Rj.mal. maṭṭī ‘kiss’, G. mukkō ‘kiss’, M. mukā and Jaṭ. makho ‘a kiss’, Bhil. mukō, makū ‘kiss’, P. miṭṭhī, S. miṭhī, G. mīṭhī, M.kas. mutti all ‘kiss’. In addition Kul. māpī ‘kisses’ and In.sir. mughī ‘kisses’. Cf. also Ta. muttu ‘kiss’. (b) Some more distantly related allomorphs are H. babbī ‘kiss’, Td. pɔ, po ‘a kiss’, Jaṭ. happā, happī ‘kiss’ and similar B.roh. appá and appwá ‘kiss’, Kann. papu ‘kiss’ and Psht. pupaī ‘a kiss on the cheek’; Kṭg. bhòbəṛ and Him. bhubri both ‘mouth (contemptous)’ — P. būbā ‘the mouth, the face of a child’ — Kal. biv ‘mouth’. (c) Similar sounding Deshi Prakrit muddā and budī ‘kiss’ (Bhayani [1988: 36]) are ← Dravidian, cf. e.g. above-quoted Ta. muttu, muttam ‘kiss’ (DEDR 4960). (d) Many IE and other languages contain a word for ‘kiss’ beginning with bu- or pu- (IEW: 103 PIE *bu- ‘lip, kiss’), some also with mu-, plus an affricate or a sibilant, pointing to onomatopoeic origin: Middle Ir. bus, pus ‘lip’, busóc, pusóc ‘kiss’, Modern Pers. bōsīdan, Lith. bučiúoti ‘to kiss’, German Buss(i), English buss, Swedish puss, Latin basium, French baiser, bec, Galician bico ‘kiss’, Zaz. p’a č‘kiss’ (with glottalized stop), etc. Several of these are derived by Pokorny < PIE *bu- ‘kiss’ ‘as imitation of the kiss sound’, cf. also PIE *pukˆ- ‘to en- close, press together’ with Albanian puth ‘kiss’. Even though there is a clear onomatopoeic background to the above ‘kiss’ words, it is remarkable that the forms found with Pokorny have in South Asia parallels almost only in the west and northwest, that is mostly in the Outer Languages whereas in the Inner Languages derivations < OIA cumba- ‘kissing’ (4868) prevail (but there is also much overlapping). This shows that there was an innovative introduction of an onomatopeic form in the Inner Languages – according to Southworth (2005a: 76) ← Proto-Dravidian *cu(m)ppu ‘to suck’ (DEDR 2621b) – which cannot be compared with forms outside this area. Therefore a PIE origin for the above- discussed forms cannot be excluded although they got hopelessly scrambled with indigenous forms. (e) Regardings Southworth’s claim of Dravidian origin for OIA cumba-, note, however, also the following Austro-Asiatic words: Bahnaric Tampuan cum ‘kiss’ and Katu cɛm ‘kiss, sniff’; Monic Nyah Kur hɤ́m ‘cuddle and kiss vigorously’, Car hamkuː ‘kiss’, Vietnamese ôm ‘kiss’, and Palaungic Danaw kᵊmu¹ ‘to kiss; to smell’. They strongly suggest ultimate Austro-Asiatic origin. Above forms beginning with m- like G. mukkō ‘kiss’, etc. have plenty of parallels in Bahnaric languages as e.g. in Laven, Cheng, Brao, Alak, Oi, Nyaheun muk all ‘kiss’. Stray cases of several of the above forms are also found in (adjacent) Tibeto-Burman languages.
